title: Coming of age
hook: at thirteen for boys, and twelve or thirteen for girls, one becomes responsible for the commandments

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was learning is sweet: honey on a slate, and a child's first letters. What did you pair your learning with? Today, years later, that child is a teenager. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

A question with a surprising answer. A Jewish boy turns thirteen. His family has no money for a party, no time to prepare, and the synagogue is closed that week for repairs. No speech. No DJ. No one even remembers it's his birthday until dinner. Is he bar mitzvah? Yes. Fully. The day he turns thirteen, by Jewish law, it has already happened. The ceremony people picture is a celebration of something that comes with the calendar, not something the ceremony creates. Today's word is what changed that morning.
screen: `NO PARTY, NO SPEECH.` → `IS HE BAR MITZVAH?` → `YES. IT ALREADY HAPPENED.`

segments.voice: Bar mitzvah. A son of the commandment; for a girl, bat mitzvah, a daughter of the commandment. Turn it four ways. First, the age. Judah ben Tema's map of a life in Pirkei Avot, the one that opened this block, has a stage that reads: at thirteen, for the commandments. For girls, the Mishnah treats twelve as the age of adulthood, and in Orthodox communities a girl becomes bat mitzvah at twelve; in some other communities, the celebration comes at thirteen, like a boy's. Second, what changes. Before this, a child is taught and encouraged, and parents carry the responsibility. After this, the young person carries it. Keeping Shabbat, fasting on Yom Kippur, counting in a prayer quorum, in communities that count them: these now belong to them. The word mitzvah means commandment. To be its son or daughter is to be the one it's addressed to. Third, the father's line. Traditionally, when a son becomes bar mitzvah, the father says a short blessing thanking God for releasing him from responsibility for this one's deeds. It can sound cold. Read another way, it's a handover, out loud. The father says, in effect: from today, your choices are yours. The blessing comes from a midrash on Jacob and Esau, twins who walked the same road until thirteen and then went their separate ways. Fourth, the party. Celebrations have grown large in some places, and they can be joyful. But the party is not the point. The point is a young person standing up, responsible now. Tomorrow, what they do with that, in front of everyone.
screen: `AT THIRTEEN, FOR THE COMMANDMENTS.` · `THE RESPONSIBILITY PASSES.` · `THE FATHER'S BLESSING.` · `THE PARTY IS NOT THE POINT.` · then, large: `RESPONSIBLE NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on one responsibility. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a moment someone handed you something for good. A key, a job, a person to care for, a decision that was now yours. Who handed it over? Did they say it out loud, or did it just happen? Then come to the present. Name one responsibility you carry today that is fully yours, that no one else will pick up if you don't. Hold it without judging how well you carry it. If you pray, you can ask for strength to carry it. The bell holds the time.
Bar mitzvah. Son of the commandment, and bat mitzvah, daughter of the commandment: the age when responsibility passes from parent to child. Today's word.
Your line: responsible now. Today, do the responsibility you named without being reminded, before anyone has to ask. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Jews become bar or bat mitzvah by age: thirteen for boys, and twelve or thirteen for girls depending on the community. Many mark it with a synagogue ceremony and a celebration, though the status comes with the age itself.

it comes with the age; the ceremony celebrates it.

original.note: Aramaic bar, son, with Hebrew mitzvah, commandment.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bar mitzvah is a big party at thirteen.
what it means: the age when responsibility for the commandments passes from parent to child; the party is optional.
what a scholar hears: Avot's 'thirteen for the commandments,' the Mishnah's twelve for girls, and a father's blessing of release.

notes: Avot 5:21 (numbered 5:24 or 5:25 in some editions) paraphrased: 'at thirteen, for the commandments'.
Girls' age: Mishnah Niddah 5:6 treats twelve as the age of a girl's vows; Orthodox practice of bat mitzvah at twelve and 'many other communities' at thirteen stated with hedges. Confirm.
Father's blessing (Baruch shepetarani) described as 'in many communities'; the link to Genesis Rabbah 63:10 (Jacob and Esau parting at thirteen) is attributed to 'a midrash'. Confirm.
Counting in a minyan 'in communities that count them' covers differences on counting women; confirm wording.
Hook scenario is illustrative. 'Celebrations have grown large in some places' kept general; confirm tone.
Original note: 'bar' is Aramaic for son; confirm.

Editor pass: 'the morning he turns thirteen' now 'the day' (the status does not wait for morning); the Avot age map is named as Judah ben Tema's from day 1291 rather than retaught; cut 'many other communities' and 'in many communities'; 'It isn't' (telling the listener what to think) now 'Read another way'; the father's blessing is correctly sourced to the Genesis Rabbah 63:10 midrash rather than 'drawing on' it.
